items.prompt: What is a 'reference architecture' most precisely?
choices: Any diagram a senior engineer drew for a past project
A named, documented blueprint for a recurring problem shape, with known trade-offs already worked out
The specific architecture one particular company happens to run in production
A mandatory standard every team in an organization must follow
items.explanation: A reference architecture is the distilled, reusable shape underneath many companies' versions of the same recurring problem — not one company's specific system, and not a mandate. It's a documented starting point, not a rule.
items.reference:
Recurring problem shape
↓
Named, documented pattern
↓
Adapted to your actual constraints

Why: the catalog entry is a starting structure with the failure modes already priced in, not a finished design.

items.prompt: A team implements a durable outbox table and calls it 'our custom notification system.' Per L1, what would change if they instead called it 'a transactional outbox, our version'?
choices: Nothing — naming is not part of the skill
Nothing changes in the code, but the name now points a future reader (or the team itself) straight at the known failure modes and trade-offs already documented for that shape
It would require rewriting the implementation to match a stricter standard
It would make the system incompatible with other patterns
items.explanation: Naming the catalog entry doesn't change the code — it changes what a future reader can look up. 'Our custom notification system' hides the shape; 'transactional outbox' surfaces it, along with every known pitfall someone else already wrote down.
items.reference:
Recurring problem shape
↓
Named, documented pattern
↓
Adapted to your actual constraints

Why: the catalog entry is a starting structure with the failure modes already priced in, not a finished design.

items.prompt: Per L1's opening scenario, what did the team actually pay for by designing a replayable notification system from a blank page?
choices: Nothing — a from-scratch design is always cheaper long-term
Three sprints re-deriving failure modes (duplicate delivery, ordering, retries) that an existing catalog entry already documents
A licensing fee for using a known pattern
Extra code review time only
items.explanation: The cost wasn't writing code — it was the sprints spent rediscovering failure modes (duplicates, ordering, retries, replay) that were already catalogued. That's the rediscovery cost a reference architecture exists to avoid.
items.reference:
🛑 Rediscovery cost

re-deriving known failure modes

📚 Lost vocabulary

3 sentences instead of 1 name

items.prompt: Besides the time spent, what is the second cost L1 names for solving a known problem shape from scratch?
choices: Legal risk from patent infringement
Losing a shared vocabulary — 'we built a thing that logs and replays state changes' takes a paragraph, where a catalog name takes three words
Losing access to open-source libraries
Reduced test coverage
items.explanation: A catalog name is compressed, shared vocabulary. Skipping it doesn't just cost design time — it costs every future explanation of the system an extra paragraph instead of a lookup-able name.
items.reference:
🛑 Rediscovery cost

re-deriving known failure modes

📚 Lost vocabulary

3 sentences instead of 1 name

items.prompt: Does using a documented reference architecture mean the team never has to think through failure modes themselves?
choices: Yes — the catalog entry guarantees correctness automatically
No — it means the well-known failure modes for that shape are already priced in and documented, but the team still adapts and verifies the pattern against their own constraints
Yes, but only for patterns published by a cloud vendor
No — catalog entries are purely theoretical and don't address failure modes at all
items.explanation: A catalog entry starts the team ahead — it doesn't finish the job. The known failure modes are documented, but applying the pattern correctly to a specific system's constraints is still real work (L2 and L3 dig into that adaptation step).
items.reference:
🛑 Rediscovery cost

re-deriving known failure modes

📚 Lost vocabulary

3 sentences instead of 1 name

items.prompt: A system must tell other systems a state change happened, without ever losing the notification even if a downstream service is down for hours. Which catalog entry does this shape match?
choices: Circuit breaker
Transactional outbox + event log
Pipe-and-filter
Strangler fig
items.explanation: 'Reliable, replayable notification of a state change' is precisely the shape the transactional outbox + event log pattern names — the write and the notification commit together, and downstream consumers pull at their own pace.

Reliable state-change notificationOutbox + event log

Layered architecture
Cache-aside
Event sourcing
items.explanation: Multiple services, one business transaction, no shared database, and a need to undo earlier steps on failure — that's exactly the shape the Saga pattern (with compensating actions) is catalogued for.

choices: Circuit breaker
CQRS

Saga
items.explanation: A flaky dependency risking cascade failure — requests piling up until resources are exhausted — is exactly the shape a circuit breaker is catalogued to fail fast against, instead of letting timeouts stack up.

items.prompt: How does a reference architecture (e.g. 'outbox pattern') differ from an architectural style (e.g. 'layered' or 'microservices')?
choices: They're the same thing with different names
A style is a broad category chosen for a whole system; a reference architecture is a specific, catalogued solution to a specific recurring sub-problem that can show up inside any style
A reference architecture always requires microservices
A style only applies to frontend systems, a reference architecture only to backend systems
items.explanation: Style is the broad, whole-system category. A reference architecture is narrower and can live inside any style — 'how do I reliably notify other systems of a change' has its own catalogued answer regardless of whether the rest of the system is layered or microservices.
items.reference:
Style: whole-system category (layered, hexagonal, event-driven, microservices)
Reference architecture: catalogued answer to one recurring sub-problem, fits inside any style

items.prompt: A microservices system and a layered monolith both need to reliably notify downstream consumers of a state change. Per L1, would they reach for different reference architectures?
choices: Yes, always — reference architectures are specific to one style
Not necessarily — the outbox + event log pattern solves that sub-problem regardless of whether the surrounding system is a monolith or split into services
Yes, because reference architectures only apply to microservices
No, because style and reference architecture are the same concept
items.explanation: Reference architectures address a sub-problem shape, not a whole-system category — a monolith with a database and a microservices system can both use a transactional outbox for the same reason, because the sub-problem (reliable notification) is identical in both.
items.reference:
Style: whole-system category (layered, hexagonal, event-driven, microservices)
Reference architecture: catalogued answer to one recurring sub-problem, fits inside any style

items.prompt: Which of these is a real, publicly documented source of reference-architecture patterns mentioned in this unit?
choices: A private internal wiki with no public equivalent
Martin Fowler's Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (PoEAA)
A single company's unpublished internal design doc
A patent filing
items.explanation: PoEAA is a well-known, publicly available catalog of data-access and domain-logic shapes — exactly the kind of documented source this unit points to instead of rediscovering patterns from scratch.
items.reference:
📚 PoEAA — data-access and domain shapes
✉️ Enterprise Integration Patterns — messaging shapes
☁️ Cloud vendor reference architecture centers — deployable blueprints

items.prompt: What kind of source is a cloud provider's 'well-architected framework' or reference architecture center best used for?
choices: Fine-grained, code-level object patterns like Gang of Four's
End-to-end deployable blueprints for a whole system shape, described with concrete managed-service names
Only frontend component styling
Legal compliance checklists exclusively
items.explanation: Cloud vendor reference architecture centers document complete, deployable system blueprints tied to their own managed services — a different granularity than PoEAA's data-access patterns or GoF's object-level ones.
items.reference:

✉️ Enterprise Integration Patterns — messaging shapes

items.prompt: Where would you look first for a catalogued Saga or circuit-breaker pattern, per L1's list of sources?
choices: Gang of Four's original Design Patterns book
microservices.io / distributed-system pattern catalogs (Saga, CQRS, circuit breaker, strangler fig)
A frontend component library's changelog
A CSS framework's documentation
items.explanation: Distributed-system patterns like Saga, CQRS, circuit breaker, and strangler fig are catalogued specifically in service-decomposition resources like microservices.io — a more specific fit than the object-level Gang of Four catalog.

items.prompt: Per L2, what signal actually justifies reaching for CQRS?
choices: A report is slow to load
Reads and writes need structurally different shapes, not just 'reads feel slow'
The team wants to use a trendy pattern
The database has more than one table
items.explanation: A slow report is a performance symptom that a database index might fix for free. CQRS earns its cost specifically when the write model and read model need genuinely different shapes — that's the signal, not raw slowness.
items.reference:
SignalPoints toward
Reads/writes need different shapesCQRS
State must be provably rebuilt from historyEvent sourcing
Change must survive a down consumerTransactional outbox

items.prompt: A team adds a missing index and a slow report becomes fast. Did they need CQRS?
choices: Yes, and they should still add it for consistency
No — the symptom (slow report) resolved with a query-tuning fix, which means the actual signal for CQRS (structurally different read/write shapes) was never present
Yes, because any slow report always indicates a shape mismatch
It's impossible to know without adding CQRS anyway
items.explanation: If a plain index fix resolves the slowness, the read and write models were never structurally different — the actual CQRS signal was absent, and the report was a data-access problem, not an architecture problem.
items.reference:
SignalPoints toward
Reads/writes need different shapesCQRS
State must be provably rebuilt from historyEvent sourcing
Change must survive a down consumerTransactional outbox

items.prompt: Per L2's compliance scenario, what actually distinguishes 'add a history table' from 'this needs event sourcing'?
choices: Whether the team likes the term 'event sourcing'
Whether the current state only occasionally needs a backward look (history table is fine) versus must always be provably reconstructable from the full history (event sourcing's actual shape)
Whether the database is SQL or NoSQL
Whether the system has more than one service
items.explanation: A history table treats the past as an occasional-lookup byproduct. Event sourcing treats the past as the primary fact the present is derived from — the signal is how strict and structural the 'must be reconstructable' requirement actually is, not which name sounds more rigorous.
items.reference:
🏷️ History table

past as occasional lookup

📜 Event sourcing

present derived from full history

items.prompt: A regulator requires that any account's state at any past date be provably reconstructable from stored facts, not just occasionally looked up. Which reference architecture's assumption does this match?
choices: Circuit breaker
Event sourcing — the current state is a derived side effect of a full, ordered history
Pipe-and-filter
Layered architecture
items.explanation: 'Provably reconstructable at any past date' is precisely event sourcing's core assumption — current state is a computed side effect of replaying the full ordered history, not a separately maintained shortcut.
items.reference:
🏷️ History table

past as occasional lookup

📜 Event sourcing

present derived from full history

items.prompt: If an app only occasionally needs to show 'what changed last week' in a support ticket, does that alone justify full event sourcing per L2?
choices: Yes, any historical lookup requirement means event sourcing

No — an occasional, non-provable backward look is closer to a simple history/audit table; event sourcing's signal is the current state being structurally derived from history, not an occasional lookup feature
Yes, because event sourcing is always the safer default
No, because event sourcing can never be used for support-ticket features
items.explanation: An occasional 'what changed' lookup is a much weaker signal than 'the current state must always be derivable from history.' The former fits a lighter audit/history table; reaching for full event sourcing here would be adopting more mechanism than the actual requirement calls for.
items.reference:
🏷️ History table

past as occasional lookup

📜 Event sourcing

present derived from full history

items.prompt: What specific signal points toward the Saga pattern, per L2's table?
choices: The system has a slow database query
One business transaction touches several services with no shared database
The team wants to reduce the number of services
Reads and writes need different shapes
items.explanation: Saga's shape is specifically for a business transaction that spans multiple services without a shared database — that's the signal that distinguishes it from, say, CQRS or event sourcing.
items.reference:
SignalPoints toward
Multi-service transaction, no shared DBSaga
Independent transformation stepsPipe-and-filter
Flaky dependency risks cascadeCircuit breaker

items.prompt: A checkout process calls payment, inventory, and shipping services in sequence, and any of them can fail after an earlier one already succeeded. What's missing if the team just calls them in sequence with no other design?
choices: Nothing — sequential calls are already a saga
A compensating action for each step, which is the actual mechanism a saga provides — without it, an earlier success is never undone on a later failure
A shared database across all three services
A faster network connection
items.explanation: A saga's value is entirely in its compensating actions. Calling services in sequence without an undo path for a partial failure is exactly the broken state a saga exists to prevent.
items.reference:
SignalPoints toward
Multi-service transaction, no shared DBSaga
Independent transformation stepsPipe-and-filter
Flaky dependency risks cascadeCircuit breaker

items.prompt: A team says 'we implemented a saga' but their checkout flow has no compensating action for a failed shipping step. Per L2, what did they actually adopt?
choices: A correctly implemented saga, just with a minor gap
The name, not the pattern — a saga without compensating actions is just calling services in a row and hoping none fail
A different, equally valid pattern called 'best-effort transaction'
An event-sourced system
items.explanation: This is L2's cargo-cult warning in miniature: the label 'saga' was borrowed, but the mechanism that makes a saga actually handle partial failure — compensating actions — was skipped.
items.reference:
SignalPoints toward
Multi-service transaction, no shared DBSaga
Independent transformation stepsPipe-and-filter
Flaky dependency risks cascadeCircuit breaker

items.prompt: What signal in a problem points toward the pipe-and-filter pattern?
choices: Data flows through several independent transformation stages that should stay testable and swappable on their own
Reads vastly outnumber writes
A flaky downstream dependency needs to fail fast
The system needs an audit trail of every change
items.explanation: Pipe-and-filter's signal is a pipeline of independent transformation stages — each filter stays testable and replaceable in isolation, which is the property the pattern is catalogued to provide.
items.reference:
Parse
→
Validate
→
Transform
→
Load

Why: each stage can be tested, replaced, or reordered without touching the others.

items.prompt: A batch ETL job parses a file, validates rows, transforms fields, then loads them into a warehouse, with each stage owned by a different sub-team. Which pattern's assumptions does this match?
choices: Pipe-and-filter
CQRS
Strangler fig
Circuit breaker
items.explanation: Independently owned, independently testable transformation stages chained together is exactly pipe-and-filter's shape — each stage (parse, validate, transform, load) can be swapped or reordered without touching the others.

items.prompt: Per L2, why doesn't picking the right catalog entry finish the design job?
choices: Because catalog entries are usually wrong
Because a catalog entry describes the shape of a class of problems, not a specific system's exact constraints — real decisions (retention, granularity, delivery mechanism) are still left
Because catalogs are only theoretical and were never actually implemented anywhere
Because reference architectures require rewriting from scratch anyway
items.explanation: A catalog entry is a starting structure with known trade-offs, not a finished design — the specific constraints of a system (how long to retain data, which fields need the guarantee, push vs. poll) are still decisions the team has to make.
items.reference:
Catalog entry: class of problems, known trade-offs
↓
Your system: specific retention, granularity, delivery decisions still needed

items.prompt: A team correctly identifies 'event sourcing' as the right catalog entry for a compliance system, then ships it without ever deciding a retention period. What's missing?
choices: Nothing — identifying the right pattern is the whole job
The adaptation step — even a correctly matched pattern still leaves real decisions (like retention) that the catalog entry doesn't make for you
A different pattern entirely
A rename to 'CQRS' instead
items.explanation: Matching the shape correctly is necessary but not sufficient — retention, granularity, and delivery mechanism are exactly the kind of system-specific decisions a catalog entry leaves open, and skipping them isn't 'done,' it's unfinished.
items.reference:
Catalog entry: class of problems, known trade-offs
↓
Your system: specific retention, granularity, delivery decisions still needed

choices: Using too many diagrams
Treating the pattern's name as the finish line instead of the start of the real design conversation
Choosing a pattern that's too old
Asking for a second opinion from another team
items.explanation: L2 names this directly: the most common misuse is stopping at the name — assuming picking the right catalog entry is the whole job, rather than the starting point for the constraint-specific decisions still ahead.

items.prompt: Implement `recordStateChange(store, orderId, toState)` for a transactional outbox: it must look up the order's current state in `store.orders`, then atomically (in one `store.transaction` call) update the order's state AND push an event object `{ orderId, fromState, toState }` onto `store.outboxRows`. Use the provided in-memory `store` shape below (already given in starter code) — do not add a separate, un-atomic call to record the event.

tests.description: updates the order's state
tests.expr: const store = { orders: { o1: { state: 'created' } }, outboxRows: [], transaction(fn) { fn(); } }; recordStateChange(store, 'o1', 'shipped'); expect(store.orders.o1.state).toBe('shipped')

tests.description: records exactly one outbox row with correct fields
tests.expr: const store = { orders: { o1: { state: 'created' } }, outboxRows: [], transaction(fn) { fn(); } }; recordStateChange(store, 'o1', 'shipped'); expect(store.outboxRows.length).toBe(1)

tests.description: outbox row captures the correct fromState and toState
tests.expr: const store = { orders: { o1: { state: 'created' } }, outboxRows: [], transaction(fn) { fn(); } }; recordStateChange(store, 'o1', 'shipped'); expect(store.outboxRows[0]).toEqual({ orderId: 'o1', fromState: 'created', toState: 'shipped' })

tests.description: both the state update and the outbox row happen inside the transaction function
tests.expr: let calls = 0; const store = { orders: { o1: { state: 'created' } }, outboxRows: [], transaction(fn) { calls++; fn(); } }; recordStateChange(store, 'o1', 'shipped'); expect(calls).toBe(1)

items.explanation: The whole point of the outbox pattern is that the state update and the event write can never be split across two separate commits — if they were, a crash between them would leave the state changed with no event recorded (or vice versa), which is exactly the bug the pattern exists to eliminate. Wrapping both writes in one `store.transaction()` call is what makes them succeed or fail together.
items.reference:
BEGIN TX: update order state + insert outbox row
↓
COMMIT — both succeed or both roll back

Why: splitting the two writes across separate commits reopens exactly the lost-notification bug the pattern exists to close.

items.prompt: Implement `markPublished(store, subscriberResults)` for an outbox publisher: given `store.pendingRows` (an array of `{ id: string }` rows) and `subscriberResults` (an array of booleans, one per row, `true` meaning every subscriber accepted that row), move only the rows whose result was `true` into `store.publishedIds` (an array of `id` strings), in the same order they appeared in `pendingRows`. Rows with a `false` result must stay out of `publishedIds` so the next poll retries them.

tests.description: marks only the fully-delivered row as published
tests.expr: const store = { pendingRows: [{ id: 'a' }, { id: 'b' }], publishedIds: [] }; markPublished(store, [true, false]); expect(store.publishedIds).toEqual(['a'])

tests.description: marks all rows published when all succeed
tests.expr: const store = { pendingRows: [{ id: 'a' }, { id: 'b' }], publishedIds: [] }; markPublished(store, [true, true]); expect(store.publishedIds).toEqual(['a', 'b'])

tests.description: marks no rows published when all fail, leaving them for retry
tests.expr: const store = { pendingRows: [{ id: 'a' }, { id: 'b' }], publishedIds: [] }; markPublished(store, [false, false]); expect(store.publishedIds).toEqual([])

tests.description: preserves original row order among published ids
tests.expr: const store = { pendingRows: [{ id: 'x' }, { id: 'y' }, { id: 'z' }], publishedIds: [] }; markPublished(store, [true, false, true]); expect(store.publishedIds).toEqual(['x', 'z'])

items.explanation: A row only counts as published once every subscriber has accepted it — leaving a partially-delivered row out of publishedIds is what makes the next poll retry it instead of silently dropping a notification a downstream service never actually received. This is the retry-until-acknowledged half of the outbox pattern, distinct from the atomic-write half tested elsewhere.
items.reference:
BEGIN TX: update order state + insert outbox row
↓
COMMIT — both succeed or both roll back

Why: splitting the two writes across separate commits reopens exactly the lost-notification bug the pattern exists to close.

items.prompt: Implement `runSaga(steps)` where `steps` is an array of `{ forward: () => boolean; compensate: () => void }`. Run each step's `forward()` in order. If a `forward()` returns `false`, stop running further steps and call `compensate()` on every step that already succeeded, in REVERSE order (most recently succeeded first). Return `true` if every step succeeded, `false` otherwise.

tests.description: returns true when every step succeeds, with no compensation calls
tests.expr: const log = []; const steps = [1,2,3].map(n => ({ forward: () => { log.push('f'+n); return true; }, compensate: () => log.push('c'+n) })); expect(runSaga(steps)).toBe(true)

tests.description: compensates already-succeeded steps in reverse order on a failure
tests.expr: const log = []; const steps = [ { forward: () => { log.push('f1'); return true; }, compensate: () => log.push('c1') }, { forward: () => { log.push('f2'); return true; }, compensate: () => log.push('c2') }, { forward: () => { log.push('f3'); return false; }, compensate: () => log.push('c3') } ]; runSaga(steps); expect(log).toEqual(['f1','f2','f3','c2','c1'])

tests.description: returns false when any step fails
tests.expr: const steps = [ { forward: () => true, compensate: () => {} }, { forward: () => false, compensate: () => {} } ]; expect(runSaga(steps)).toBe(false)

tests.description: never calls compensate on a step whose forward() itself failed
tests.expr: const log = []; const steps = [ { forward: () => true, compensate: () => log.push('c1') }, { forward: () => { log.push('f2-ran'); return false; }, compensate: () => log.push('c2') } ]; runSaga(steps); expect(log).toEqual(['f2-ran','c1'])

items.explanation: A saga's defining mechanism is the reverse-order compensation on failure — each step that already committed gets explicitly undone, most-recent-first, so a partial failure never leaves the system in a half-committed state. The step that itself failed never gets compensate() called, since its forward() never actually took effect.
items.reference:
charge card
→
reserve stock
→
schedule ship — fails

Why: undo runs in reverse: un-reserve stock, then refund the card — most recent first.

items.prompt: Implement `firstFailureIndex(steps)` where `steps` is an array of `{ forward: () => boolean }`. Run each step's `forward()` in order, stopping as soon as one returns `false`. Return the index of the first step that returned `false`, or `-1` if every step succeeded. Do not run any step after the first failure.

tests.description: returns -1 when all steps succeed
tests.expr: expect(firstFailureIndex([{forward: () => true}, {forward: () => true}])).toBe(-1)

tests.description: returns the index of the first failing step
tests.expr: expect(firstFailureIndex([{forward: () => true}, {forward: () => false}, {forward: () => true}])).toBe(1)

tests.description: does not run steps after the first failure
tests.expr: let ran = []; const steps = [ {forward: () => { ran.push(0); return true; }}, {forward: () => { ran.push(1); return false; }}, {forward: () => { ran.push(2); return true; }} ]; firstFailureIndex(steps); expect(ran).toEqual([0,1])

tests.description: returns 0 when the very first step fails
tests.expr: expect(firstFailureIndex([{forward: () => false}, {forward: () => true}])).toBe(0)

items.explanation: A saga has to know exactly where it stopped succeeding before it can compensate correctly — running every step regardless of failure, or continuing past the first failure, would either waste side effects or make the reverse-compensation order wrong. Stopping immediately at the first false is what a real saga orchestrator does before it starts undoing anything.
items.reference:
charge card
→
reserve stock
→
schedule ship — fails

Why: undo runs in reverse: un-reserve stock, then refund the card — most recent first.

items.prompt: Implement `compensationOrder(succeededCount)` which, given how many steps already succeeded (as an integer `succeededCount`), returns an array of the zero-based indices of those steps in the order their `compensate()` should be called — most recently succeeded first. For example, if 3 steps succeeded (indices 0, 1, 2), compensation should run on index 2, then 1, then 0.

tests.description: returns indices in reverse for 3 succeeded steps
tests.expr: expect(compensationOrder(3)).toEqual([2, 1, 0])

tests.description: returns a single index for 1 succeeded step
tests.expr: expect(compensationOrder(1)).toEqual([0])

tests.description: returns an empty array when nothing succeeded yet
tests.expr: expect(compensationOrder(0)).toEqual([])

tests.description: returns indices in reverse for 5 succeeded steps
tests.expr: expect(compensationOrder(5)).toEqual([4, 3, 2, 1, 0])

items.explanation: Compensation always unwinds most-recent-first, the same reason a stack unwinds in reverse push order: the last step to succeed is the one whose side effects are freshest and most directly need undoing before earlier steps' effects are touched. This is the same ordering `runSaga` relies on internally, isolated here as its own small, testable piece.
items.reference:
charge card
→
reserve stock
→
schedule ship — fails

Why: undo runs in reverse: un-reserve stock, then refund the card — most recent first.

items.prompt: Per L3, why did the order-notification team NOT build a full event-sourced read model on top of the outbox, even though the shape looked adjacent to event sourcing?
choices: Event sourcing is never compatible with an outbox
None of their 3 consumers needed to reconstruct arbitrary past state — only the current state plus the specific change fact — so a full read-model layer would solve a problem they didn't have
It was too expensive to license
The database didn't support it technically
items.explanation: L3 is explicit: building a full CQRS/event-sourced read-model layer would have been over-adaptation — solving 'reads and writes need different shapes,' a signal this system never actually exhibited. Matching the catalog entry doesn't mean adopting every adjacent pattern too.
items.reference:
DecisionWhy
6-month retention, not indefiniteAudit requirement is bounded
No full event-sourced read modelNo consumer needs arbitrary past-state reconstruction
Polling, not push3 known consumers — a broker was unneeded surface

items.prompt: Why did the team retain outbox events for 6 months instead of indefinitely, per L3?
choices: Storage was too expensive to store any events at all
The audit requirement was explicitly bounded at 6 months — an indefinite log would be cost the actual requirement never asked for
The pattern requires exactly 6 months of retention by definition
Regulators forbid keeping data longer than 6 months in all cases
items.explanation: Retention is a config decision the catalog entry leaves open — this team set it at 6 months because that's what the actual audit requirement specified, not because the pattern mandates any particular retention window.
items.reference:
DecisionWhy
6-month retention, not indefiniteAudit requirement is bounded
No full event-sourced read modelNo consumer needs arbitrary past-state reconstruction
Polling, not push3 known consumers — a broker was unneeded surface

items.prompt: Why did the team choose a 2-second polling interval instead of a message-broker push, per L3?
choices: Polling is always technically superior to push
With only 3 known consumers, a broker's operational surface was unneeded cost — polling was cheap enough and simple enough to operate for that scale
Message brokers cannot deliver events reliably
The outbox pattern requires polling by definition
items.explanation: This is another adaptation decision, not a mandate from the pattern: with 3 known consumers, the added operational complexity of a broker wasn't justified by the actual scale. A system with many more consumers or a tighter latency need might reasonably choose differently.
